reason: The sources thoroughly document the timeline, the immediate political fallout, the famous trial, and the modern exoneration of the alleged arsonist, providing more than enough cross-referenced claims.
story: On the night of February 27, 1933, Berliners saw the Reichstag—the home of German democracy—engulfed in flames. Chancellor Adolf Hitler, in power for only four weeks, arrived quickly and declared it a "sign from God." Police arrested Marinus van der Lubbe, a sweaty, unemployed Dutch laborer found on the scene with firelighters. Although Van der Lubbe claimed he acted alone to inspire a workers' uprising, Hitler instantly blamed a massive Communist conspiracy. By morning, President Hindenburg signed an emergency decree suspending all civil rights, allowing police to arrest thousands of opponents. This "temporary" decree lasted for twelve years, enabling the Nazis to dismantle democracy and pass the Enabling Act. While Van der Lubbe was convicted and beheaded, his co-defendants were acquitted. It took seventy-five years for Germany to posthumously pardon him, recognizing that his conviction by a Nazi court defied basic justice.
angle: The emergency decree signed the morning after the Reichstag fire, which suspended Germany's core civil liberties to 'protect' the public, was never repealed and remained the legal basis of Hitler's dictatorship until the fall of Nazi Germany in 1945.

claims.claim: The fire took place on the evening of February 27, 1933, causing severe damage to the Reichstag building in Berlin.
Adolf Hitler had been appointed Chancellor of Germany on January 30, 1933, just weeks before the incident.
Pedestrians outside the Reichstag building around 9:00 p.m. heard breaking glass right before flames erupted.
Marinus van der Lubbe, a 24-year-old unemployed Dutch laborer, was caught and arrested at the scene.
The Nazis immediately blamed the fire on a Communist conspiracy and portrayed it as the start of an uprising.
On February 28, 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree into law.
The Reichstag Fire Decree suspended core constitutional rights, including freedom of speech, assembly, and the press.
The decree gave the police authority to arbitrarily arrest political opponents and ban opposition publications.
In the aftermath of the fire, thousands of Communists and political opponents were arrested and rounded up by authorities.
A major trial was held in Leipzig later in 1933, prosecuting Van der Lubbe alongside German and Bulgarian Communists.
Van der Lubbe was the only defendant convicted, while the other co-defendants were acquitted due to lack of evidence.
Van der Lubbe was sentenced to death and executed by beheading in January 1934.
On March 23, 1933, the German parliament passed the Enabling Act, which gave Hitler full legislative powers.
Decades later, the German government officially pardoned Van der Lubbe under a 1998 law.
Willi Münzenberg led an independent investigation that produced 'The Brown Book,' a bestseller arguing that Van der Lubbe was a Nazi pawn.

disputed: Whether Marinus van der Lubbe acted alone or had Nazi accomplices is heavily debated; some historians support the single-perpetrator theory while others suggest a Nazi conspiracy or cover-up.
The 1955 affidavit of SA member Hans-Martin Lennings, claiming the fire was already burning when they arrived with Van der Lubbe, is treated as a newly surfaced historical debate.
Hermann Göring's alleged 1943 boast that he set the fire was denied by Göring under cross-examination at Nuremberg; a script should present this as an unproven allegation.
